sections.title: How does the Hydraulic jump calculator work?
sections.html:
The Hydraulic jump calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports discharge (Q) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the gravitational acceleration (g), the channel width (B), the upstream depth (y₁) and the upstream velocity (v₁).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hydraulic jump calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Discharge (Q)=channel width (B) × upstream velocity (v₁) × upstream depth (y₁)
Downstream velocity (v₂)=discharge (Q) ÷ (channel width (B) × downstream depth (y₂))
Upstream Froude number (F₁)=upstream velocity (v₁) ÷ the square root of (gravitational acceleration (g) × upstream depth (y₁))
Downstream Froude number (F₂)=downstream velocity (v₂) ÷ the square root of (gravitational acceleration (g) × downstream depth (y₂))
Downstream depth (y₂)=depth ratio (y₂ ÷ y₁) × upstream depth (y₁)
Upstream Froude number (F₁)=(1 ÷ 2) × the square root of (2) × the square root of (depth ratio (y₂ ÷ y₁) × (depth ratio (y₂ ÷ y₁) + 1))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Gravitational acceleration (g) = 9.8067 m/s², Channel width (B) = 30 m, Upstream depth (y₁) = 30 m and Upstream velocity (v₁) = 10 m/s. Working through the relationship above gives Discharge (Q) = 900 m³/s, Upstream Froude number (F₁) = 1.619, Downstream depth (y₂) = 55.327 m and Downstream velocity (v₂) = 5.422 m/s.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Discharge (Q) = 900 m³/s, Upstream Froude number (F₁) = 1.619, Downstream depth (y₂) = 55.327 m and Downstream velocity (v₂) = 5.422 m/s should be roughly the size you expected from Gravitational acceleration (g) = 9.8067 m/s² and Channel width (B) = 30 m.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Acceleration, opening in meters per second squared
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Flow rate, opening in cubic meters per second
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Length, opening in meters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Hydraulic jump calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the gravitational acceleration, the channel width and the upstream depth — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the Hydraulic jump calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns discharge (Q), derived from the gravitational acceleration, the channel width and the upstream depth. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Hydraulic jump calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the gravitational acceleration, the channel width, the upstream depth and the upstream velocity, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter gravitational acceleration (g) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Gravitational acceleration (g) opens in meters per second squared and the chip beside it offers 5 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Discharge (Q) = 900 m³/s. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Hydraulic jump calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
